extracted.intended_audience: students of algebraic geometry (advanced undergrad/graduate), Math 216 course participants
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and theorems for when morphisms (especially to projective space) are closed embeddings, behavior and vanishing of higher direct image (pushforward) sheaves, and numerical/cohomological criteria for line bundles on projective curves (base-point-freeness, separation of points/tangents, very ampleness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre's cohomological characterization of affineness
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Noetherian separated scheme X the following are equivalent: (a) X is affine; (b) for any quasicoherent sheaf F on X, Hi(X,F)=0 for all i>0; (c) for any coherent sheaf of ideals I on X, H1(X,I)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes (a)⇒(b)⇒(c) are straightforward; the substantive content is (c)⇒(a). Analogy: Stein spaces in complex analytic geometry satisfy a similar cohomological vanishing characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic properties of higher direct image sheaves (Riπ_* )
rubrics_metrics.description: If π:X→Y is quasicompact separated and F quasicoherent on X, then Riπ_*F is a quasicoherent sheaf on Y and: (a) Riπ_* is a covariant functor QCoh(X)→QCoh(Y); (b) R^0π_* = π_*; (c) a short exact sequence on X induces a long exact sequence of the R^iπ_* on Y; (d) if π is projective and F coherent (and O_Y coherent), then each R^iπ_*F is coherent on Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as Theorem 18.8.1. Use Cech computations on affines and localization to check properties; (d) is Grothendieck's coherence for projective morphisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanishing of higher pushforwards for affine π
rubrics_metrics.description: If π is affine then for i>0, Riπ_*F = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as an easy exercise (18.8.A); this is the immediate special case of the definition/behaviour of pushforwards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base change morphism and cohomology commutes with affine flat base change
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a Cartesian square with π:X→Y and ψ:Z→Y, there is a natural map ψ^*(Riπ_*F) → R^iπ'_* (ψ'^*F); if ψ is affine and flat (or satisfies the flatness hypotheses in the exercise), this map is an isomorphism (cohomology commutes with affine flat base change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints reference the FHHF (finite hypercover/flatness) theorem and reducing to i=0 (push-pull) cases; Exercise 18.8.B treats this and Exercise 18.8.C suggests further generalization via Leray spectral sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection formula (relative version)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural morphism (R^iπ_*F) ⊗ G → R^iπ_*(F ⊗ π^*G) for π:X→Y and quasicoherent F on X, G on Y; if G is locally free then this morphism is an isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 18.8.E; the FHHF Theorem is suggested in the hint. Use this when pulling factors through pushforwards in projective/flat situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative dimensional vanishing
rubrics_metrics.description: If π:X→Y is projective and Y locally Noetherian (or O_Y coherent), then R^iπ_*F = 0 for i greater than the maximum dimension of the fibers of π.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Theorem 18.8.5. The statement can fail without projectivity (an explicit counterexample is given in Exercise 18.8.F). The proof reduces locally on Y and uses affine-cover vanishing on fibers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative Serre vanishing
rubrics_metrics.description: If π:X→Y is proper of Noetherian schemes and L is π-ample, then for any coherent F on X, R^iπ_*(F ⊗ L^{3 m}) = 0 for all i>0 and m sufficiently large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 18.8.G; this generalizes Serre vanishing to the relative (family) setting and is useful to make higher pushforwards vanish after twisting by high powers of a relatively ample line bundle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grothendieck's Coherence Theorem (for proper morphisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π:X→Y is proper and Y locally Noetherian, then for any coherent sheaf F on X, each R^iπ_*F is a coherent sheaf on Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as Theorem 18.9.1. The proof (sketched) uses Chow's Lemma and the Leray spectral sequence to reduce to the projective case (where coherence was proven earlier). Useful for translating projective results to proper morphisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chow's Lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a proper morphism π:X→Spec A with X Noetherian, there exists a projective surjective morphism µ:X'→X such that π ������� �������◦µ is projective and µ is an isomorphism on a dense open subset of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as Theorem 18.9.2. Chow's Lemma is the tool to reduce proper to projective situations; the text includes exercises guiding the explicit construction (closures in products of projective spaces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for a morphism to be a closed embedding (Theorem 19.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let k be algebraically closed. If π:X→Y is a projective morphism of finite-type k-schemes that is injective on closed points and induces injective maps on tangent vectors at closed points, then π is a closed embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a practical criterion to show a map from a variety/curve to projective space is a closed immersion: check pointwise injectivity and injectivity on tangent spaces. The text warns both hypotheses are necessary (examples: normalization of a cusp, Frobenius map, and a non-projective counterexample in Figure 19.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite morphism of degree 0 or 1 at every point implies closed embedding (Theorem 19.1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π:X→Y is finite and the degree of π at every point of Y is either 0 or 1, then π is a closed embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text reduces Theorem 19.1.1 to this statement: unramified + finite = closed embedding in the Noetherian setting. Exercises show this implies injectivity on points and isomorphism on residue fields and tangent spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative-degree line bundles have no nonzero sections
rubrics_metrics.description: For a projective geometrically integral curve C, if L is an invertible sheaf with deg L < 0 then h^0(C,L)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: any regular (global) section would give zeros minus poles equal to deg L; if deg<0 a regular section cannot exist. This is an elementary but frequently used fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree-0 line bundles: h^0 is 0 or 1 and triviality criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: If deg L = 0 on a geometrically integral projective curve C, then h^0(C,L) is 0 or 1; moreover if h^0(C,L)=1 then L  OC (i.e., L is trivial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: a nonzero section has no zeros or poles so div(s)=0 and L OC; geometric integrality ensures h^0(OC)=1. Use base-field extension as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-degree h^0 formula (Riemann-Roch consequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: If L is an invertible sheaf on a genus g curve C and deg L > 2g-2 then h^0(C,L) = deg L - g + 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Serre duality to see h^1(C,L)=0 when deg L>2g-2 (since L^\vee ⊗ ω_C has negative degree), then apply Riemann-Roch. The page flags this as an important formula to remember.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twisting by a degree-1 point changes h^0 by at most 1
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is a closed point of degree 1, then h^0(C,L) - h^0(C,L(-p)) equals 0 or 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the exact sequence 0→L(-p)→L→L|_p→0 and the fact h^0(L|_p)=1. This controls how the space of sections changes when imposing a vanishing at a point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical criterion for base-point-freeness on curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Over an algebraically closed field, if for every closed point p of C we have h^0(C,L) - h^0(C,L(-p)) = 1, then L is base-point-free (i.e., has no base points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because for each p there is a section not vanishing at p. This gives a morphism C→P^{h^0(L)-1} by Theorem 16.4.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for separating points in the linear series
rubrics_metrics.description: If p and q are distinct closed points and h^0(C,L) - h^0(C,L(-p-q)) = 2, then the linear series |L| separates p and q (i.e., the associated morphism sends p and q to distinct points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, there exist sections distinguishing p and q because the two imposed conditions decrease h^0 by 2; this is the standard separation-of-points test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for separating tangent vectors
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is a closed point of degree 1 and h^0(C,L) - h^0(C,L(-2p)) = 2 then the map associated to L separates tangent vectors at p (i.e., the differential is injective there).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This condition guarantees existence of a section vanishing to order exactly 1 at p (not order 2), which yields a nonzero cotangent pullback, hence surjectivity on cotangent space (equivalently injective tangent map).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical criterion for very ampleness on curves
rubrics_metrics.description: If for all pairs of closed points p,q (possibly equal) on C we have h^0(C,L) - h^0(C,L(-p-q)) = 2, then L is very ample and the associated map is a closed embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combines the base-point-free, separation-of-points, and separation-of-tangents criteria and invokes Theorem 19.1.1 (injectivity on points and tangent vectors implies closed embedding for projective morphisms over algebraically closed fields).
